reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it presents a creator-hosted giveaway offering a $50 Ulta gift card in exchange for subscriptions, notifications, likes, a comment, and a contact method. The presenter displays a basket and an Ulta-branded card, and the specified winner-contact channels serve as an anti-impersonation warning. The evidence does not show payment, asset transfer, sensitive-credential collection, or a completed loss, although it does not establish whether the prize was ultimately awarded.

comment your instagram handle so that I will be able to contact you, if you do not have an instagram then comment your best email to be reached at.
Last but not least and the main thing in this. Giveaway is a $50 gift card to Ulta.
so in this basket you have all the rest of the prizes

opening.argument: The central offer is a low-barrier reward tied directly to a sequence of viewer actions. Entry requires subscribing, enabling notifications, liking the video, commenting, and supplying an Instagram handle or email address. In return, the participant is promised a $50 Ulta gift card and additional prizes. That is not merely discussion of a gift card; it is a solicitation in which engagement and contact information are the stated pathway to a chance at the reward. The video therefore fits a reward-acquisition pattern even though no payment is requested.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The fact that the reward is described as a giveaway does not remove the solicitation. The stated rules expressly condition entry on subscription, notifications, liking, commenting, and providing a contact method. Calling those actions ordinary engagement does not answer the underlying concern: the promised reward is used to obtain them, while the evidence does not establish that any winner actually received it.

citations.quote: follow all of the steps and you will be entered to win this giveaway
This giveaway will end October 15th

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The quoted rules show an engagement promotion, but they do not show that participants paid, surrendered an account, or transferred an asset. The reward is a chance to win, not a guaranteed payout, and the stated process says the winner will be chosen randomly. The contact information is requested for winner notification, not shown being used for theft or a fraudulent claim flow.

the only email I will contact you from is [EMAIL] and the only instagram I will dm you from is @alexaharpp
know that is the winner they email. Me back or uh dm me back on instagram

opening.argument: Several risk signals appear together: a valuable branded gift card, multiple additional prizes, a deadline, and a request for an email address or Instagram handle. The offer is presented as easy to obtain through routine online actions, while the winner-contact process depends on personal contact details and a later response. The description even emphasizes that only particular accounts will contact entrants, highlighting an impersonation-sensitive channel. These features create a persuasive acquisition funnel around a gift-card reward, and the supplied material does not independently establish delivery of the promised prize.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The anti-impersonation warning does not eliminate the other signals; it confirms that contact after entry is an important part of the process. A deadline and a branded gift card can increase pressure and perceived legitimacy, while the description still requests an email or social-media handle. The absence of a documented loss does not prove the promised reward process was genuine.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: These are ordinary safeguards and contest mechanics, not evidence of deception. The warning tells entrants which channels are authentic, the deadline defines when entries close, and the description identifies a random-generator selection. The material shows no request for money, passwords, payment credentials, or external verification, and it does not show a fraudulent contact or an unpaid winner.

opening.argument: The casual presentation as a thank-you video obscures that the content functions primarily as a channel-growth promotion. The creator links the offer to reaching a subscriber milestone, asks viewers to subscribe and activate notifications, and says the rules will be followed for entry. The basket display and gift-card presentation make the promotion concrete and encourage participation, but they do not establish that the reward will be delivered. Thus, the ordinary-giveaway framing should be understood as the promotional wrapper around a reward-for-engagement solicitation.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling it a thank-you does not change the operative structure: the rules say viewers must complete engagement steps to be entered, and the creator says the video is showing the prizes. The basket and visible card make the offer more persuasive, but displaying items is not proof that a randomly selected entrant will receive them. The promotional framing is therefore relevant to how participation is solicited.

Showing the prizes and asking for channel engagement are consistent with a creator-hosted promotion; they do not show a fraudulent acquisition scheme or any completed harm.
